subject: [PATCH] mm: memcg: use ratelimited stats flush in obj_cgroup_may_zswap()

reviews.author: Yosry Ahmed
reviews.summary:
Reviewer Yosry Ahmed noted that the original mechanism used in commit 42a300353577 had issues with atomic updates on all parents, leading to inaccurate reads by up to MEMCG_CHARGE_BATCH * nr_cpus * nr_children, and proposed a different approach where the update side always iterates per-CPU counters in all parents and the read side always iterates per-CPU counters in this cgroup for accuracy.

Reviewer noted that decompression is a performance-critical code path and expressed concern about potential regression from using ratelimited stats flush

Reviewer Yosry Ahmed pointed out that the proposed approach's main concern is read latency, not update latency, and suggested that if it works for in-kernel consumers, it should also work for userspace consumers.
reviews.raw_body:
IIUC, in that commit, the update side modifies one per-CPU per-cgroup
counters, and when those counters exceed a threshold atomic updates
are performed on all parents, which I think is the slow side. Then,
the read side just reads the potentially stale atomic. That was
problematic because:
(1) The update side can end up performing atomic updates on all parents.
(2) The read side can be inaccurate by up to MEMCG_CHARGE_BATCH *
nr_cpus * nr_children

What I am proposing in (c) is different:

(1) The update side always updates per-CPU per-cgroup counters in all
the parents. It never does atomic operations. The parent iteration is
not cheap, but it is cheaper than atomics for sure and we already do
parent iteration today in some cases in memcg_rstat_updated(). So the
"slow" path should be the same as today.
(2) The read side always iterates per-CPU counters in this cgroup, so
it's always accurate. This might be more expensive on an rstat flush
on average (e.g. if memcg_vmstats_needs_flush() skips the flush), but
it is much more consistent and the tail latency is much better.

---

Well, decompression is in the fault path, that's performance critical
to some extent (although not like other stats updated by networking).
Anyway, I think the update path shouldn't regress much with the
approach described in (c).

---

I think in the proposed approach (c) the main concern is actually read
latency, not update latency. So if it works for in-kernel consumers it
should definitely work for userspace consumers as well?

reviews.author: Shakeel Butt (author)
reviews.summary:
Author addressed Yosry Ahmed's concern about performance impact of memcg_rstat_updated by explaining that the parent traversal is short-circuited when the flush threshold is hit, but acknowledged significant CPU usage at Meta scale.

Author responded to concerns about the suitability of ratelimited stats flush for zswap, stating that it's unclear whether this approach will work and suggesting that evaluation is needed at production scale rather than through benchmarks.

Author responded to concerns about performance impact of ratelimited stats flush, explaining that decompression and minor page faults are on micro-second and nano-second scales respectively, making the upward traversal cheap.

Author responded to Yosry Ahmed's concern about the performance implications of using a ratelimited stats flush in obj_cgroup_may_zswap(). The author explained that they were mainly thinking about kernel consumers which have strict staleness requirements, and that rstat flushing is more expensive than their proposed mechanism. They also suggested that once this special mechanism is implemented, it could potentially replace the existing ratelimited flush code.
reviews.raw_body:
Yes but that parent traversal is short circuited when we hit the flush
threshold. At Meta scale, we have observed significant cpus being spent on
memcg_rstat_updated before that.

---

It might be or not. Usually such things are more clear at scale in production
instead of benchmarks.

---

Decompression is on the scale of micro-seconds (and I suspect the simple minor
page faults are on nano-seconds scale) and the upward traversal is definitely
much cheaper and will be a noise there.

---

Here I was mainly talking about consumers which has more strict staleness
requirements and those are mainly kernel consumers. Rstat flushing is definitely
more expensive than this for-each-cpu traversal and most of the time they just
need it for one or very small set of stats.

I am imagining once we have this special mechanism for selected stats, we can
potentially remove ratelimited flush and stats update threshold code.

reviews.author: Yosry Ahmed
reviews.summary:
Reviewer questioned whether the upward per-CPU traversal is indeed expensive, suggesting that it might be caused by concurrent flushers and cache line bouncing

reviewer expressed hope for transitioning all stats flushing to the new scheme if it works well and suggested collecting production data to inform the decision
reviews.raw_body:
Interesting. So the upward per-CPU traversal takes time? Perhaps due
to concurrent flushers causing the cachelines to bounce?

---

Yeah that's the hope. I was basically saying that I am hoping for
more, to transition everything to this flushing scheme if it works
well.

Anyway, as you mentioned, ideally we need production data to proceed.
Joanne, is this something that you are trying to collect by any
chance? :)

2026-08-26.patch_summary: This patch modifies the obj_cgroup_may_zswap() function to use a rate-limited statistics flush instead of the current approach, which is expensive for kernel consumers that require strict staleness. The change aims to reduce the overhead of memcg_rstat_updated and make it more efficient at scale in production environments. By introducing a special mechanism for selected stats, the patch potentially paves the way for removing rate-limited flush and statistics update threshold code altogether.
